entry.title: Is evolution defied because life is an “idea”?

link.title: Is evolution defied because life is an “idea”?

entry.content:
Eric Hedin had a post at Science & Culture Today (The Discovery Institute’s former Evolution News) that seems to fully commit to Platonic idealism and to teleology. Which is surprising since he is a Ph.D. in particle physics, from my own University. It will be found here.

Its final two paragraphs will give you the general drift, but you should read Hedin’s post, which is short:

To imagine that each of the millions of species of living creatures on Earth “evolved” by a weeding-out process, undirected by any idea of the wholeness they would ultimately manifest, runs counter to our experience with functional design and the known limitations of the laws of nature. If prolific reproductivity is the “goal” of natural selection, why should life have ever evolved to anything beyond bacteria? Cancer cells, as a mutation from original design, would seem to be evolution’s crowning achievement.

The wholeness of living organisms testifies to their metaphysical origin as an “idea,” originating in the mind of their Maker. The evidence suggests that creatures exceed the boundaries of what is possible by undirected natural forces. Even information, as we understand it, appears to fall short as the groundwork for life. Apparently, life comes from life, and nothing else will suffice. Life is a brilliant idea!

Is there some way we can counter this argument? The title of his article is “In Defiance of Evolution, Life is an Idea”. Is evolutionary biology finally totally defied?

entry.title: Two decades ago, Dover showed how to win elections in conservative towns. They're still fighting

link.title: Two decades ago, Dover showed how to win elections in conservative towns. They're still fighting

entry.content:
Lauri Lebo is an advocacy coordinator and organizer for the Pennsylvania State Education Association. As a reporter, she covered the Kitzmiller v. Dover trial and wrote a book about her coverage, The Devil in Dover. She is a recipient of NCSE’s Friend of Darwin award in 2026. We asked her to write a few paragraphs linking to her recent article in the Reviews Reports of the National Center for Science Education. – Matt Young

It’s been 21 years since the First Amendment test case of Kitzmiller v. Dover, in which U.S. District Court judge John E. Jones III ruled that “intelligent design,” a form of revamped creationism, is unconstitutional to teach in the public schools.

While the parents who sued and science teachers celebrated, the school board members and their legal team had little to say. Looking back, most people involved in the trial said that few minds were changed. Many were just glad the national spotlight was no longer shining on Dover.

But roots run deep in south-central Pennsylvania, and history repeats itself. Some on the religious right quietly started preparing for the next opportunity.

I still get asked about comparisons between Kitzmiller v. Dover and attacks today on our public schools. Particularly, what did we learn about defeating school boards pushing a religious agenda? In this article in the Reviews Reports of the National Center for Science Education, I delve into what worked then and what works today.

entry.title: Zeugomantispa minuta
entry.content:
Photography Contest.

Al Denelsbeck, Runner-up.


Another optics problem! The submission was by design relatively low in resolution, so I asked for the original and cropped it so as to reveal more information. More below the fold. Hard to say, but it looks to me like the diffraction pattern of a hexagonal array, probably seen as an image in the “len” formed by the eye (a “len” is half a thin lens). I would have expected it to be rotated by 30°, though, and the colors in the secondary maxima do not look right. Maybe someone else can weigh in.
entry.summary: Photography Contest. Al Denelsbeck, Runner-up. Zeugomantispa minuta – northern green mantidfly. Mr. Denelsbeck writes, "I was delighted to find a northern green mantidfly having only spotted one over a decade previously, and captured this one for a studio session. However, two different lenses captured two different effects from the compound eyes under near-identical conditions and lighting. The left version is with a reversed 28-105 lens at approximately F/16 with a custom softbox on the flash, from a very short distance, while the right is with a 180 mm macro, also at F/16 and the same softbox, but significantly greater working distance. I have not yet determined if the different effects were from the working distance and perhaps diffusion of the lighting (the left version being more diffuse because the softbox was more above the subject and broader in 'source,') or it was a product of the optics of the two lenses - the 28-105 lens was never intended to be used in reverse, and might have suffered from the methods used to reduce chromatic aberration. The right version is much more stunning, but also a bit distracting. My subject was released back where found after the session. Overall body length just 12 mm. Another optics problem! The submission was by design relatively low in resolution, so I asked for the original and cropped it so as to reveal more information. More below the fold.

entry.title: An unhappy birthday: Lamarck is misrepresented

link.title: An unhappy birthday: Lamarck is misrepresented

entry.content:
Today (August 1) is the 282nd birthday of Jean-Baptiste Pierre Antoine de Monet, the Chevalier de Lamarck. He died in 1829, so we do not have him here to answer questions about his thought. To me he was the first evolutionary biologist, even if his mechanism for adaptation was mistaken.

Sadly, his work has often been misunderstood, and is still being described incorrectly today. He invoked two mechanisms of evolutionary change. One was a general tendency for organisms to get more complex. This must have seemed like a possibility back in 1800, at the height of the Romantic era, when grand trends of nature were in fashion.

The other is his mechanism of Use and Disuse. Organisms that made more use of particular organs or features thereby influenced their hereditary substances to have those be bigger and stronger in their offspring. Note that this is not the same as having the effects of the environment influence the hereditary substances. It is the will of the organism that does the job, not just the direct effect of the environment.

There are increasing numbers of misunderstandings of Lamarck’s theories.

Epigenetics?

The discovery of “epigenetic” modifications of genes, ones which can be influenced by the environment has led enthusiasts for them to declare that they vindicate Lamarck’s theory.
Here are some interpretations of Lamarck along those lines promoted by the Discovery Institute

  • Michael Flannery, a historian associated with the old-earth creationist site Reasons To Believe, posted this at Science && Culture Today: https://scienceandculture.com/2026/07/re-evaluating-lamarcks-contribution-to-evolutionary-thought/

  • Andrew Macdiarmid, a Discovery Institute staff member, has posted here promoting a book on the role of epigenetics by Thomas Woodward and James Gillis, published this year by Discovery Institute Press.

There are a number of other books arguing that evolutionary biologists have been neglecting Lamarckian mechanisms:

Eva Jablonka has written or edited a quite a few books arguing that. Here is an edited volume on this.

Pim Edelaar has recently published a book calling for evolutionary biology to be reconceived with Lamarckian mechanisms in a central role. Here is a post at The Conversation in which he summarizes the book.

And here is an article on a new book by Jessica Riskin arguing that Lamarckian thought should be given a central place in evolutionary biology.

I think that all this is wrong. Let’s discuss …

entry.title: Despite the Failure to Meet Attendance Projections, the Kentucky GOP Loves Ark Encounter

link.title: Despite the Failure to Meet Attendance Projections, the Kentucky GOP Loves Ark Encounter

entry.content:
Reprinted with permission from the blog Righting America.

Recently, Answers in Genesis CEO Ken Ham has produced a lot of propaganda celebrating the fact that the Ark has been open for 10 years in July. Propaganda that fails to acknowledge that the Ark has never come close to the 1.2 to 2.2 million annual visitors projected by Answers in Genesis.

But in early July, an Ark representative gave questionable testimony about Ark attendance to the Kentucky Legislature Committee on Tourism. A few days later the Kentucky House GOP posted this video to YouTube. Apparently, Representative Kim King once counted 15 out of state license plates in the Ark parking lot!

Wowie!

The purpose of the Tourism committee meeting – which consisted primarily of Ark propaganda – is unclear. Could the long-term goal be to give the Ark more tax incentives or some other Kentucky taxpayer money? At about 44 minutes in the Ark’s representative claims a million visitors a year, while Dr. William Trollinger, based on information from my monthly Kentucky Open Records Act requests, demonstrates the Ark has never come close to their attendance projections that were made when bullying the state, Grant County, and the City of Williamstown out of perks to build the Ark. (Note: These numbers don’t include free admission for children under 10 and yearly or lifetime pass holders.)

In June 2026, the Ark sold 96,004 tickets according to my monthly Kentucky Open Records Act request. This is up 4,520 tickets compared to June of last year, but much lower than 2024 numbers. Although this is better than last year’s precipitous drop, it is still not good news for the Ark.

Because the Ark will have been open ten years, it means the Ark’s $1.825 million/year sales tax incentive rebate will expire either in July, 2027 or at the end of the fiscal year. How will they adapt to losing this annual chunk of change from the Commonwealth of Kentucky’s teat? Will they get a Christian Nationalist legislator or perhaps a future Republican Governor to help them find more money from Kentucky’s treasury? (Perhaps a tax incentive package for their long-planned Tower of Babel reconstruction and ride?)

I predict, at a minimum, the Ark will go from for-profit to non-profit so they won’t have to pay Williamstown the safety-fee money. Thus, Williamstown and Grant County will be on the hook for police, fire, and infrastructure costs for a non-profit ministry that once promised them streets of gold.

With gasoline and other expenses soaring, it will be interesting to see how the Ark amusement park fares in remaining summer months. Despite low ticket sales, the Ark and Answers in Genesis seems awash in cash. The Ark opened a new “Welcome Center” for visitors in March, presumably with more opportunities for visitors to spend money. It is amusing to see how outrageously expensive admission has become (adult 1 day tickets are approximately $55) and how the operators find new ways to all but vacuum money out of visitor’s pockets with extras such as the virtual reality rides ($16.50), zip lines ($59 to $144), tree sloth experience ($60), macropod (kangaroo and wallaby) experience ($40), bird of prey experience ($50), camel encounter ($5), mining sluice (mineral and fossil bags) ($10 to $55), plus guided Ark tours ($25), and parking ($15).

In any case, these numbers indicate that the Ark will never come near the 1.2 to 2.2 million projected by Answers in Genesis when they were begging and bullying for financial perks from various governmental entities.

P.S., by William Trollinger [publisher of Righting America]

I am sure it goes without saying that Ken Ham never acknowledges how Ark attendance has fallen far short of the projections made when, to quote Dan Phelps, “bullying the state, Grant County, and the City of Williamstown out of perks to build the Ark.” According to those projections, Ark attendance in Year 8 of its existence would have been at just about 2.5 million; at 682,101 visitors, the Ark reached but 27% of its projected attendance.

This failure to come close to their own attendance predictions may explain why Ken Ham has taken to making the case that The Ark Encounter, which teaches the gospel clearly through various exhibits, attracts many non-Christian visitors – they make up about 30% of its total visitors – and our extensive guest surveys reflect that an estimated 70,000+ people a year trust Christ for salvation as a result of their visit. I would call that a fantastic investment in people’s eternity.

Oh my. Here are just a few observations about Ham’s claim:

  1. Sue Trollinger and I have visited the Ark numerous times, and the notion that 30% of Ark visitors (in year 8,204,630 individuals) are “non-Christian” seems, well, ludicrous. Listening to our fellow visitors, and talking with others who have visited the Ark, it has been obvious that the vast majority of folks in attendance are evangelicals and fundamentalists. Of course, these numbers come from Ham and company, and besides everything else, they are the ones deciding which folks qualify as “non-Christian.” (Fundamentalists who have “backslidden,” perhaps?)
  2. Accepting their numbers as legitimate, this would mean that in Year 8 61,389 individuals decided to “trust Christ for salvation as a result of their visit.” Again, this seems, well, ludicrous. Again, these numbers come from Ham and company. But perhaps the Ark’s extreme emphasis on Hell – represented here by the global Flood which (according to Ark placards) drowned up to 20 billion (billion, not million) individuals – so frightened 61,839 individuals in Year 8 that they claimed a religious experience. Maybe it is like the camps I attended as an adolescent, when the sermons on hell inevitably resulted in evangelical teenagers (often the same teenagers, year after year after year) streaming forward to “rededicate” their lives to Christ.
  3. The overwhelming emphasis on Hell makes obvious what sort of “gospel” the Ark is teaching so “clearly.” A gospel of eternal torture for the vast majority of human beings. Sermon on the Mount? Matthew 25? Not so much.

entry.title: Araneus diadematus
entry.content:
Photography Contest.

Gert Korthof, Winner.

The remaining two photographs:

And the remainder of the commentary:

In macro photographs of single threads of the web, many differently colored, sharply defined transverse bands are revealed. Are they real or just optical illusions? If they are illusions, why do we see an almost endless row of transverse bands instead of a continuous light spectrum like a rainbow? It is hard to believe that sunlight can produce these in a homogeneous fiber. Instead it seems more reasonable to assume that fine-meshed transverse bands do exist along the length of the thread and have different structural biochemical properties. Because these threads are of biological origin, I expect that these bands or stripes can be explained by different protein contents (spidroins). In short: I think the cross-transverse bands are real and not optical illusions, although the exact colors are caused by optical effects and depend on the direction of the light rays.

I shall add that the web was most likely backlighted, rather than, as I had initially assumed, frontlighted, like a rainbow. I had initially thought that the color was due to dispersion, but possibly it is diffractive. Dietrich Zawischa gives a general, qualitative explanation here. See also here.
entry.summary: Photography Contest. Gert Korthof, Winner. Araneus diadematus – garden cross spider. Dr. Korthof writes: "Spiderwebs are completely invisible and very difficult to detect, except when the sun shines on the web at a certain angle. Then colors similar but not identical to rainbow colors can be observed. The pictures show the web of the garden cross spider, also known as the European garden spider." I have taken the liberty of grouping his three entries as one and display the remaining two below the fold.

entry.title: Can natural selection make organized complexity?

link.title: Can natural selection make organized complexity?

entry.content:
A previous PT post here discussed philosopher of science Joseph K. Cosgrove’s review of William Dembski and Winston Ewert’s 2nd edition of The Design Inference. I had some qualms and questions about Cosgrove’s conclusions. I hoped he would comment in the discussion. He was kind enough to contribute a substantial argument in the conmments section of that post. This included responses to my and John Harshman’s comments on his argument.

(For more links to the earlier posts on reviews of Dembski and Ewert’s book, and to Cosgrove’s review, see the link I just gave.)

In response to John Harshman’s comment Cosgrove commented:

On John H’s remark about my “trichotomy” of chance, necessity, and design: To our knowledge, blind processes in nature produce two kinds of outcomes: Chance produces random outcomes and necessity produces ordered outcomes. Both chance and necessity are involved in both types, but the outcomes still can be categorized in terms of one or the other. A roll of the dice, for instance, follows the laws of physics and so conforms to necessity, but it produces a chance outcome governed by a probability distribution. By contrast, the atoms of a chemical crystal have to line up in a deterministic pattern dictated by the equilibrium of forces. That is a necessary outcome although it also involves chance (which particular atoms end up where, for instance). Neither of these two types is organized (a sequence of coin tosses is complex but not organized; a chemical crystal is ordered, not organized). So my trichotomy is really chance, necessity, and organized complexity. If there is a fourth category in addition to chance, necessity, and organization I’m not aware of what it is.

To our knowledge, no mere combination of chance and necessity can produce organized complexity.

John Harshman then said:

Then one must ask what natural selection consists of and whether it is so capable.

I think this exchange is particularly important in evaluating Cosgrove’s argument, so I have put up this post, in hopes that Cosgrove, Harshman, and our other commenters can address this issue.
